title: Architecture Review & Refactoring
readme:
FULL STACK DEVELOPER 2026 - Phase 35
Architecture Review & Refactoring

This phase pauses feature development to review TaskFlow as one system. It includes focused books, a combined book, architecture/dependency rules, an ADR template, a prioritized refactoring backlog template, review checklists, and verification assets.

lessons.body:
Full-System Architecture Inventory
Before changing architecture, document what actually exists. Review runtime boundaries, dependency direction,
ownership, and operational dependencies instead of relying on an idealized diagram from an earlier phase.

-       API client /      -                          -                         -                      -         Prisma /
Next.js                                            NestJS                    Services             Repositories
>         Query           >                          >                         >                      >        PostgreSQL

Figure 2 - Primary request path under review

Runtime inventory
• Next.js 16: authenticated application UI, Server Components, forms, URL state, TanStack Query client regions.

• NestJS 12 + Fastify: HTTP boundary, authentication, authorization, application services, exception handling.

• Prisma 7.9.1 + PostgreSQL: persistence and relational constraints.

• Supabase: Auth, managed PostgreSQL, Storage, Realtime; not the owner of TaskFlow business rules.

• GitHub Actions, Docker, deployment platforms, Sentry/telemetry: delivery and operations boundaries.

Review artifact
• Record each boundary, its public contract, dependencies, and data ownership.

• Compare the current codebase with the intended architecture; the difference is useful evidence, not failure.
Architecture review begins with the system you actually have, not the system you remember building.
Source basis: integrated TaskFlow architecture and engineering decisions established in Phases 00-34; this chapter is an internal
review/refactoring synthesis rather than a new framework feature.

lessons.title: Dependency Direction and Accidental Coupling
lessons.summary: Dependency Direction and Accidental Coupling Dependencies should point toward the layer that owns the contract. A useful review looks for framework details leaking upward, business decisions leaking downward, and shared packages importing application-specific code. - - Persistence - Infrastructure HTTP / UI Application intent >…
lessons.body:
Dependency Direction and Accidental Coupling
Dependencies should point toward the layer that owns the contract. A useful review looks for framework details leaking
upward, business decisions leaking downward, and shared packages importing application-specific code.

-                            -       Persistence         -      Infrastructure
HTTP / UI              Application intent
>                            >        contract           >     implementation

Figure 3 - Desired direction: outer mechanisms depend on inner contracts

Healthy examples
• TasksService depends on TaskRepository contract, not Prisma query shapes.

• Controllers depend on application services, not database clients.

• The web consumes API contracts, not Prisma-generated types.

• packages/validators contains transport-neutral shared validation, not NestJS decorators or React components.

Coupling smells
• A UI component imports generated Prisma enums directly.

• A repository throws NestJS HTTP exceptions.

• A shared package imports from apps/web or apps/api.

• A service accepts Fastify Request/Reply objects.

• Infrastructure credentials become arguments to domain/business helpers.
# Review question for every import
Who owns this contract?

If A imports B:
- Does A genuinely depend on B's responsibility?
- Or did a convenient type/location create accidental coupling?

Do not chase zero coupling. Chase intentional coupling with clear ownership.

lessons.body:
Controller, Service, and Repository Responsibility
Review
Phase 24 introduced repositories only after persistence complexity earned the abstraction. Phase 35 reviews whether
that boundary still helps or merely moved code into more files.

Review area                       Healthy signal                                     Refactor trigger

Controller                        HTTP mapping, validated transport input            Business rules, Prisma queries

Service                           Business workflow, invariants, orchestration       Fastify response objects, raw SQL

Repository                        Persistence query mechanics and mappings           HTTP errors, UI behavior, role policy

Repository value test
• Does it hide meaningful persistence mechanics rather than merely rename Prisma methods?

• Does it create a useful testing seam for service behavior?

• Do method names express application persistence intent such as listScoped rather than generic findAll?

• Can complex transaction requirements still be expressed without fighting the abstraction?

Service size test
• A large service is not automatically wrong; look for multiple independent reasons to change.

• Extract policy/workflow helpers only when responsibility, reuse, or testability becomes clearer.
The goal is not thin files. The goal is cohesive responsibilities.

lessons.title: Validation Contracts and Duplication Review
lessons.summary: Validation, Contracts, and Duplication Review TaskFlow intentionally validates at more than one layer. The review distinguishes necessary repeated trust checks from accidental schema duplication that can drift. - - API transport - - Browser form Shared field rules Business rules DB constraints > > schema…
lessons.body:
Validation, Contracts, and Duplication Review
TaskFlow intentionally validates at more than one layer. The review distinguishes necessary repeated trust checks
from accidental schema duplication that can drift.

-                           -       API transport         -                       -
Browser form             Shared field rules                                           Business rules          DB constraints
>                           >         schema              >                       >
Figure 4 - Different validation layers answer different questions

Keep these distinctions
• React Hook Form/Zod improves immediate user feedback.

• NestJS request validation remains the security boundary even if the browser already validated.

• Business validation checks context such as membership, due-date policy, or workflow state.

• PostgreSQL constraints protect relational integrity regardless of application bugs.

Refactor candidates
• Repeated literal field limits that represent the same transport-neutral rule can live in packages/validators.

• Do not share HTTP-only schemas if doing so leaks server concerns into the browser.

• Do not derive authorization or business policy from client-side schemas.
Duplicate validation can be correct when the layers defend different boundaries. Duplicate rules are the problem only when
they represent the same source of truth and can drift.

lessons.summary: Transactions, Business Rules, and Persistence Boundaries Transactions are one of the fastest ways an otherwise clean layering model can become dishonest. Review where atomicity actually belongs and whether repositories obscure multi-model workflows. Choose Business - Identify atomic - - - transaction Execute Commit / rollback…
lessons.body:
Transactions, Business Rules, and Persistence
Boundaries
Transactions are one of the fastest ways an otherwise clean layering model can become dishonest. Review where
atomicity actually belongs and whether repositories obscure multi-model workflows.

Choose
Business           -     Identify atomic      -                            -                         -
transaction                   Execute              Commit / rollback
operation                    writes
>                          >         boundary           >                         >
Figure 5 - Transaction boundaries follow business operations

Questions to ask
• Which business operation must succeed or fail as one unit?

• Does the current repository contract allow that transaction without exposing ORM details everywhere?

• Is a single Prisma nested write sufficient, or is an interactive transaction required?

• Are external side effects such as email/Storage incorrectly placed inside a database transaction?

Do not force purity
• If Task, Membership, and Audit writes must share one transaction, use an explicit persistence/application transaction design
rather than pretending separate repositories are isolated worlds.

• Do not add a UnitOfWork abstraction until repeated cross-repository transaction pressure proves it useful.
Transaction correctness outranks diagram purity.

Frontend State and Server/Client Boundary
Review
Volumes 06 and 07 created several legitimate state owners. Phase 35 checks for accidental duplication and
client-boundary growth after forms, TanStack Query, optimistic updates, and Realtime were added.

Review area                       Healthy signal                                     Refactor trigger

Server data                       TanStack Query / Server Component fetch            Copied into useState

URL filters                       Next.js URL/searchParams                           Hidden global store copy

Form draft                        React Hook Form                                    Query cache mutated on each keystroke

Auth session                      Supabase Auth                                      Homegrown duplicate auth store

Local interaction                 useState/useReducer                                Application-wide Context without need

Review client boundaries
• Can a component become a Server Component again?

• Did one small event handler cause an entire page tree to become use client?

• Are large libraries shipped to the browser for interactions that could be isolated or lazy-loaded?

• Does Realtime invalidate authoritative server state instead of turning WebSocket payloads into a second backend?
The browser should own interaction state, not duplicate the backend.

lessons.body:
Authentication, Authorization, and Security
Boundary Review
Security architecture is reviewed as a chain. Each layer must still make an independent, explicit decision after later
refactors and performance work.

Supabase         -                         -                         -      Membership /        -                      -        Business
JWT verification           TaskFlow User                                       Resource scope
session         >                         >                         >       permission         >                      >        operation

Figure 6 - Identity and authorization remain separate decisions

Security regression checks
• No controller accepts userId from the browser as authenticated identity.

• NestJS still verifies bearer tokens independently of the Next.js session.

• Tenant scope is part of repository/database queries before ordinary search, sorting, or pagination.

• Realtime and Storage policies do not replace NestJS business authorization.

• Service-role/database credentials remain server-only and are redacted from logs.

Refactoring rule
• When moving code, preserve the security decision point. A cleaner abstraction that accidentally broadens access is not an
architectural improvement.
Authorization is behavior. Every structural refactor needs security regression coverage.

Monorepo, Packages, Configuration, and
Boundary Review
Monorepos make sharing easy, which also makes inappropriate sharing easy. Review package direction, duplicated
configuration, environment-variable ownership, and whether the workspace structure still communicates the system
clearly.

Healthy package direction
• apps/web and apps/api may consume packages/validators.

• Shared packages should not import application entry points.

• Infrastructure/deployment files should not become runtime application dependencies.

• Version locks and environment contracts should have one documented owner.

Configuration drift checks
• Do local, CI, Docker, staging, and production use the same variable names and meanings?

• Are Prisma, Node, pnpm, and framework locks consistent across docs/workflows/images?

• Do CORS origins, Supabase redirects, health paths, and public URLs agree across deployment templates?

• Are deprecated example files still misleading learners or operators?
apps/web -----> packages/validators <----- apps/api
|                                      |
+---- no import from apps/api ---------+

shared package rule:
- reusable contract/value
- no app entrypoint dependency
- no hidden infrastructure secret

A monorepo is not permission to make every module globally reusable.

Testing, Observability, and Operational Debt
A refactor is safest when tests and telemetry cover the seams being changed. Review whether the system can prove
behavior before, during, and after restructuring.

Testing seam review
• Pure policies: fast unit tests.

• Services: fake repositories where persistence details are irrelevant.

• Repositories: real PostgreSQL integration tests.

• HTTP: authentication, authorization, validation, and error-contract E2E tests.

• Web: component/form/query tests and a small set of Playwright critical flows.

Operational debt review
• Can requestId join client reports, logs, error monitoring, and traces?

• Do readiness checks represent actual traffic readiness?

• Are deployment smoke tests still aligned with current routes?

• Do dashboards and alerts cover the business-critical path after refactors?

• Are runbooks stale or missing ownership?
If a risky area has no trustworthy test or observable signal, improving that safety net may be the first refactor.

Dead Abstractions, Overengineering, and
Simplification
A mature review removes complexity as aggressively as it adds structure. Every abstraction has carrying cost: naming,
navigation, indirection, tests, documentation, and onboarding.

-           Identify          -                              -   Keep / merge /
Find abstraction                                           Measure value
>         consumers           >                              >      delete

Figure 7 - Architecture can improve by removing layers

Candidate smells
• A repository method used once that exactly mirrors one Prisma call and adds no policy/query value.

• A Context provider with one nearby consumer.

• A mapper that copies identical fields between structurally identical objects.

• A utility package created for one function and no independent ownership.

• A generic interface introduced to support hypothetical future databases with no actual migration pressure.

Delete carefully
• Prove behavior with tests before simplification.

• Prefer a smaller explicit design over a generic framework built inside the application.

• Keep abstractions that protect valuable boundaries even when their implementation is currently simple.
The simplest architecture is not the one with the fewest files; it is the one with the fewest unnecessary concepts.

lessons.summary: Refactoring Strategy, ADRs, and Change Safety Architecture review produces a backlog, not a giant rewrite. lessons.body:
Refactoring Strategy, ADRs, and Change Safety
Architecture review produces a backlog, not a giant rewrite. Refactor one bounded pressure point at a time, record
consequential decisions, and use the existing testing/deployment system to keep changes reversible.

Problem          -                         -                          -                      -                         -        Continue /
Decision                Small change                   Tests                Observe
evidence         >                         >                          >                      >                         >          revert

Figure 8 - Safe refactoring loop

Prioritization model
• P0: correctness/security/data-loss risk.

• P1: blocks frequent change or causes repeated incidents.

• P2: meaningful maintainability/testing/performance debt.

• P3: cosmetic consistency with little practical impact.

ADR discipline
• Record context, decision, alternatives, consequences, and revisit trigger.

• Use ADRs for meaningful architecture decisions, not every small refactor.

• A decision can be superseded later; the historical reasoning remains useful.

Change safety
• One conceptual refactor per pull request when practical.

• No opportunistic behavior change hidden inside structural cleanup.

• Use feature flags or compatibility layers when migration cannot be atomic.
Refactoring should reduce uncertainty. A giant rewrite multiplies it.

The lab produces concrete review artifacts for TaskFlow and prepares the final phase. The learner should finish with a
map, prioritized backlog, explicit dependency rules, and at least one safely completed refactor.

Lab 1 - inventory

Lab 2 - score pressure points
• Choose five areas and classify: correctness risk, security risk, change frequency, test difficulty, operational pain.

• Do not rank by personal dislike of folder structure.

Lab 3 - execute one refactor
• Pick one P1/P2 item that can be changed safely.

• Add/confirm regression coverage before change.

• Refactor, run tests, smoke the relevant path, and inspect telemetry/log behavior.

Phase exit
• Architecture map matches current implementation.

• Dependency rules are explicit.

• Refactoring backlog is prioritized by evidence.

• Dead or misleading abstraction is removed or justified.

• At least one architecture decision is captured in an ADR.
Phase 35 is complete when TaskFlow is easier to explain and change - not when every file matches a textbook pattern.

Guided Build Lab — Phase 35: Architecture Review & Refactoring

Purpose
Review and refactor TaskFlow architecture using evidence: dependency direction, duplication, tests, complexity, security, and operational boundaries.

Architecture review report plus one behavior-preserving refactor backed by tests and an ADR.

Before you touch the code

Architecture trace
observe architecture -> identify smell/risk -> establish tests -> small refactor -> verify behavior -> document decision

Read this flow left to right, then right to left. For each arrow, say what data crosses the boundary, which side trusts the other, and what evidence would prove that this boundary works. This habit prevents framework APIs from becoming disconnected memorization.

Step 1 — Draw the current dependency graph from UI to database and mark places responsibilities leak across boundaries.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. Goal

lessons.body:
Debugging Workshop — Phase 35: Architecture Review & Refactoring

Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.

The debugging loop
1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action.
2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state.
3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior.
4. Form one hypothesis.
5. Change one variable.
6. Re-run the same reproduction.
7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis.

Boundary walk
observe architecture -> identify smell/risk -> establish tests -> small refactor -> verify behavior -> document decision

Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next.

Failure drill 1 — Big-bang rewrite
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 2 — Refactor with no behavioral safety net

Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — Architecture Review & Refactoring

Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 35 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?

Required outcome
Review and refactor TaskFlow architecture using evidence: dependency direction, duplication, tests, complexity, security, and operational boundaries.

Required artifact
Architecture review report plus one behavior-preserving refactor backed by tests and an ADR.

Constraints
• Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch.
• Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt.
• Keep changes scoped to the capability.
• Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases.
• Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable.

Acceptance criteria
• Can identify architectural smell with evidence.
• Can preserve behavior while refactoring.
• Can remove unnecessary abstraction.
• Can document tradeoffs in an ADR.

Independent build sequence
1. Draw the current dependency graph from UI to database and mark places responsibilities leak across boundaries.
2. Find one duplication or accidental abstraction whose cost is visible in real code.
3. Create/strengthen tests around the behavior before moving code.
4. Refactor in small commits, verifying typecheck/tests after each conceptual move.
5. Measure whether the result reduced coupling/duplication or merely moved files.
6. Write a short ADR recording context, decision, alternatives, consequences, and when to revisit.

Self-review
Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence.

Stretch challenge
Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Predict whether your design still behaves correctly. If not, document the next architectural improvement rather than adding complexity blindly.

Phase exit
Run the relevant checks, inspect Git diff, and write a three-sentence summary: what the system can do now, which boundary owns the new responsibility, and which failure you now know how to diagnose. Only then mark the phase complete.

Mastery Capstone Lab

This is the transfer exercise for Phase 35: Architecture Review & Refactoring. The detailed lessons are now closed-book reference material. Your task is to prove that the phase outcome can be reproduced from requirements, repository evidence, and debugging—not by copying a finished implementation.

Target artifact
Architecture review report plus one behavior-preserving refactor backed by tests and an ADR.

Acceptance criteria
- Write the behavior and constraints before implementation.
- Identify the owning layer and every boundary crossed.
- Implement the smallest complete vertical slice.
- Verify the happy path from outside the implementation.
- Demonstrate at least one expected failure path.
- Run the phase-relevant quality checks.
- Review the diff for accidental duplication, leaked responsibilities, missing validation/authorization, and hidden environment assumptions.

Evidence packet
Save the command/request used, expected result, actual result, one failure reproduction, the fix, and a short explanation of why the final responsibility belongs where it does. This packet is more valuable than a screenshot of a green page because it demonstrates repeatable engineering reasoning.

Stretch
Change one requirement after the first implementation. Measure which files must change. If a tiny domain change causes unrelated layers to move, use that evidence to discuss coupling before adding another abstraction.

# TaskFlow Architecture Map - Phase 35

## Primary request path

Browser -> Next.js -> authenticated API client -> NestJS/Fastify -> auth guard -> authorization -> application service -> repository -> Prisma -> PostgreSQL

## Supporting infrastructure

- Supabase Auth: external identity/session provider
- Supabase Storage: attachment bytes; PostgreSQL stores attachment meaning/metadata
- Supabase Realtime: freshness signal; HTTP/NestJS remains authoritative
- TanStack Query: browser server-state cache
- React Hook Form: unsaved form draft state
- GitHub Actions + Docker + deployment platforms: delivery/operations
- Sentry/logs/metrics/traces: observability

## Dependency rules

1. Controllers do not query Prisma directly.
2. Services own business workflow and policy decisions.

# Architecture Review Checklist

## Backend
- [ ] Controllers stay transport-focused.
- [ ] Services own business workflow/invariants.
- [ ] Repositories hide meaningful persistence mechanics.
- [ ] Transactions match business atomicity.
- [ ] HTTP exceptions do not leak into persistence adapters.

## Frontend
- [ ] Server state is not duplicated into local state.
- [ ] URL state remains deep-linkable.
- [ ] Form drafts stay in React Hook Form.
- [ ] Client boundaries are as small as practical.
- [ ] Auth/session state is not duplicated.

## Security
- [ ] Identity comes from verified token claims.
- [ ] Tenant scope is enforced server-side.
- [ ] Storage/Realtime do not replace application authorization.

# Dependency Rules

## Allowed
- apps/web -> packages/validators
- apps/api -> packages/validators
- TasksService -> TaskRepository contract
- PrismaTaskRepository -> PrismaService

## Avoid / reject
- apps/web -> apps/api source imports
- shared package -> apps/web or apps/api
- service -> Fastify Reply/Request
- repository -> NestJS HTTP exceptions
- UI -> Prisma-generated model as public API contract

Every exception should be documented with a reason and revisit trigger.

# Package Boundary Review

## packages/validators
Earned because both web and API consume transport-neutral field rules. It must not become a dumping ground for server-only DTO semantics or UI code.

## Future package rule
Create a shared package only when:
1. There are at least two real consumers or a clear independent ownership boundary.
2. The package has a coherent responsibility.
3. Moving code there reduces coupling rather than hiding it.

Do not create generic `shared`, `common`, or `utils` packages without an explicit responsibility statement.

# TaskFlow Architecture Review Snapshot

This package contains review artifacts rather than a replacement application architecture.

Use it to:
- document the current system,
- identify actual pressure points,
- prioritize debt,
- record decisions with ADRs, and
- verify refactors without changing observable behavior accidentally.

The default stance is incremental improvement, not rewrite.

# Refactoring Backlog Template

| Priority | Area | Evidence | Risk | Proposed change | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P0 | Example: tenant query | Cross-workspace test missing | Security | Add scoped repository test before any query refactor | Integration + E2E |
| P1 | Example: transaction workflow | Repeated multi-repository orchestration | Correctness | Evaluate explicit transaction boundary | Service + repository integration |
| P2 | Example: duplicated field rules | Same title limits in web/API | Drift | Move neutral field rule to validators package | Unit + form + API validation |
| P3 | Example: naming | Inconsistent helper names | Cosmetic | Rename when touching area | Typecheck/tests |

Priority is based on system pressure, not aesthetic preference.

# Source Basis

Phase 35 is an internal synthesis of the TaskFlow architecture established throughout Phases 00-34. It intentionally introduces no new framework dependency.

Review evidence should come from:
- the current repository,
- tests,
- runtime telemetry,
- deployment incidents,
- change frequency,
- security findings, and
- developer/operator friction.

If framework/provider behavior materially changes in the future, verify the relevant official documentation before altering architecture decisions based on it.

# API Review Example

Trace one endpoint end-to-end:

`PATCH /tasks/:id/status`

1. Controller: parse validated route/body and current user.
2. Authorization: verified identity and resource scope.
3. Service: status transition invariant and completedAt behavior.
4. Repository: scoped Task lookup/update query.
5. Prisma/PostgreSQL: persistence and constraints.
6. Exception filter: stable HTTP error contract.
7. Observability: requestId, timing, safe error classification.

If a responsibility appears in two incompatible owners, add it to the refactoring backlog.

# Frontend State Review Example

For `/tasks?status=DONE&page=2`:

- URL state: status=DONE, page=2
- TanStack Query: fetched page result
- React Hook Form: only create/edit draft
- Supabase Auth: session
- Local React state: menu/dialog/selection only where local
- Derived values: compute from current data; do not persist another copy

Reject any new store unless it solves a real state-ownership problem not already covered above.

| Refactor area | Minimum verification |
|---|---|
| Business policy extraction | Pure unit tests |
| Service/repository boundary | Service tests + repository integration tests |
| Tenant query restructure | Real PostgreSQL cross-workspace tests + HTTP E2E |
| Validation sharing | Browser form tests + API validation tests |
| Frontend state ownership | Component/query tests + critical Playwright flow |
| Authentication/authorization changes | 401/403/404 E2E matrix |
| Transaction changes | Integration tests with rollback/failure scenarios |
| Deployment/config refactor | CI build + staging smoke tests |
| Observability refactor | Synthetic error + requestId correlation check |
